marker_p6.coling::07106895-c293-4117-be28-f7598533: Thank you for an interesting read. item I personally like the information bottleneck item principle and am very happy to item see its application to deep neural item networks. The derivation of item the variational lowerbound is very clear, item even for those who are not item very familiar with variational inference. Also item the explanation of the IB principle item is clear. Experimental results seem to item be very promising. I found the item presentation for the model a bit item confusing. In variational inference/information maximisation, p item usually denotes the model and q item represents the "inference engine". This means item the choice of inference method is item independent to the modelling procedure. However item the presented VIB assumed p(x, y) item as the **underlying data distribution** (and item approximated by the empirical distribution), thus item here the model is actually q(y|z)p(z|x). item Then the authors presented p(y|x) as item the **predictive distribution** in page 8, item paragraph 2 of section 4.2.3. Predictive item in what sense? I guess you item meant p(y|x) = \int q(y|z) p(z|x) item dz in this case, but this item makes the two definitions contradict to item each other! The authors have made item an interesting connection to variational auto-encoder item and the warm-up training (by tuning item beta). However, even when the loss item function formula is the same to item the variational lowerbound used in VAE item (in this case beta = 1), item the underlying model is different! For item example, r(z) in VIB is the item variational approximation to p(z) (which means item r(z) is not a component in item the model), while in VAE it item is the prior distribution which is item actually defined in the modelling procedure. item Similaly p(z|x) in VIB is included item in the model, while in VAE item that is the approximate posterior and item can be independently chosen (e.g. you item can use p(x|z) as a deep item NN but p(z|x) as a deep item NN or a Gaussian process). In item summary, I think the presentation for item the modelling procedure is unclear. I item hope these point would be made item clearer in revision since the current item presentation makes me uncomfortable as a item Bayesian person. To my knowledge, this is the first paper that applies IB item to train deep networks (the original papers only presented the concept), but item see below for the note of independent work claim. The derivation of item the variational lowerbound is very clear, even for those who are not item very familiar with variational inference. Also the explanation of the IB principle item is clear. Experimental results seem to be very promising. I found the item presentation for the model a bit confusing. In variational inference/information maximisation, p item usually denotes the model and q represents the "inference engine". This means item the choice of inference method is independent to the modelling procedure. However item the presented VIB assumed p(x, y) as the **underlying data distribution** (and item approximated by the empirical distribution), thus here the model is actually q(y|z)p(z|x). item Then the authors presented p(y|x) as the **predictive distribution** in page 8, item paragraph 2 of section 4.2.3. Predictive in what sense? I guess you item meant p(y|x) = \int q(y|z) p(z|x) dz in this case, but this item makes the two definitions contradict to each other! The authors have made item an interesting connection to variational auto-encoder and the warm-up training (by tuning item beta). However, even when the loss function formula is the same to item the variational lowerbound used in VAE (in this case beta = 1), item the underlying model is different! For example, r(z) in VIB is the item variational approximation to p(z) (which means r(z) is not a component in item the model), while in VAE it is the prior distribution which is item actually defined in the modelling procedure. marker_p12.coling::d8e4451f-f606-413a-a2c5-5f2b5e9c: First up, I want to point out that this paper is really item long. Like 17 pages long -- without any supplementary material. While ICLR item does not have an official page limit, it would be nice if item authors put themselves in the reviewer's shoes and did not take undue item advantage of this rule. Having 1 or 2 pages in addition to item the conventional 8 page limit is ok, but more than doubling the item pages is quite unfair. Now for the review: The paper proposes a item new artificial dataset for sequence learning. I call it artificial because it item was artificially generated from the original MNIST dataset which is a smallish item dataset of real images of handwritten digits. In addition to the dataset, item the authors propose to train recurrent networks using a schedule over the item length of the sequence, which they call "incremental learning". The experiments show item that their proposed schedule is better than not having any schedule on item this data set. Furthermore, they also show that their proposed schedule is item better than a few other intuitive schedules. The authors verify this by item doing some ablation studies over the model on the proposed dataset. I item have following issues with this paper: -- I did not find anything item novel in this paper. The proposed incremental learning schedule is nothing new item and is a natural thing to try when learning sequences. Similar idea item have already been tried by a number of authors, including Bengio 2015, item and Ranzato 2015. The only new piece of work is the ablation item studies which the authors conduct to tease out and verify that indeed item the improvement in performance is due to the curriculum used. -- Furthermore, item the authors only test their hypothesis on a single dataset which they item propose and is artificially generated. Why not use it on a real item sequential dataset, such as, language modeling. Does the technique not work in item that scenario? In fact I am quite positive that for language modeling item where the vocabulary size is huge, the performance gains will be no item where close to the 74% reported in the paper. -- I'm not item convinced about the value of having this artificial dataset. Already there are item so many real world sequential dataset available, including in text, speech, finance item and other areas. What exactly does this dataset bring to the table item is not super clear to me. While having another dataset may not item be a bad thing in itself, I almost felt that this dataset item was created for the sole purpose of making the proposed ideas work. item It would have been so much better had the authors shown experiments item on other datasets. -- As I said, the paper is way too item long. A significant part of the length of the paper is due item to a collection of experiments

marker_p12.coling::ef4cca12-c45c-4b1b-9c67-8db766ad: Say you're a merchant living in 17th century Amsterdam, and there's a item bunch of super-rich ladies who really, really loves cumin (as in, the item spice). Unfortunately, cumin doesn't grow anywhere near Amsterdam, you have to go item to the middle east or India to get some of that fine item stuff so it's *super-expensive*. Over there, however, it grows like a weed item and costs very little money. If only you could get some of item that cheap cumin over to Amsterdam, you could make a lot of item money! Unfortunately, the only way to do that is to send out item a big-ass ship for like nine months. Not only is that HUGELY item expensive (you have to get a ship, and a captain and crew item who all wants nine months worth of pay), but it is also item really risky. The boat could sink, after all, or all the cumin item could spoil. So how do you accomplish this? Assuming you're not stupendously item rich yourself (and very few people or groups, aside from maybe whole item nations, are that rich), how do you finance this? You could go item to a bank or money-lender and take out a loan, a loan item which would have a very steep interest rate that could almost eat item up all of your profits. And what if the boat sank? You'd item be completely bankrupt, and be thrown into prison, if the money-lender doesn't item waste your broke ass first. So, you come up with an idea. item You can't finance this trip alone. But you could rather easily finance, item say, one tenth of the cost of the trip. And look at item that, you have nine friends, all of whom could also afford one item tenth of the cost of the trip. So you all come to item an agreement: you decide to each finance part of the cost for item the trip (i.e. you "buy stock" in the enterprise), each getting shares item worth one tenth of the total enterprise. With this money, you pay item for the boat and crew, send them off, and then nine months item later, it comes back with a cargo-hold full of delicious, super-expensive cumin. item The profits far and away compensate for the initial cost, and each item of you and your friends gets one tenth of the enormous profits. item But what happens if your boat sinks? Well, it's a real bummer item obviously (especially for the crew!), but you only payed for one tenth item of the cost, and this was a cost you could afford to item eat, you're not gonna get killed over it. Since the risk was item spread around to 10 people, no one landed in debtors prison. Everyone item took a small hit, instead of one person taking an enormous hit. item Think about this example, and all the people involved in it. The item fancy ladies got their cumin (and for cheaper than they would have item otherwise). The shipwrights got work building a new ship. The captain and item crew all got work and a salary. The trader in India got item a new customer for his cumin. And obviously, you and your friends item got really rich in the process. In short, *every single person is item better off*, and it wouldn't have happened if this notion of "buying item and selling stocks" didn't exist. This is the advantage of a stock item market. It moves capital around from where it just lies around doing item absolutely nothing to where it can be put to use, and in item the meantime, everybody gets richer. It also distributes risk between lots of item people, so you don't have to be afraid of going broke all item the time. Now, obviously, there are problems with how the modern day item American version of the stock market functions. But the critique is that item it stopped doing what doing what it is supposed to be doing item (i.e. allocating capital so that it can be put into productive use) item and stopped being a means to an end, and

In Grace Bros Pty Ltd v The Commonwealth (1946), Justice Dixon item stated that the inclusion of the condition was to "prevent arbitrary exercises item of the power at the expense of a State or a subject." item The interpretation of the terms "acquisition" and "just terms" by the High item Court of Australia have had the effect, however, of limiting its protection item of property rights. Moreover, it operates at any time the Commonwealth makes item a compulsory acquisition of property. As such, it is a contingent guarantee item rather than a general constitutional right or freedom to enjoy property rights. item The Commonwealth may only acquire property on just terms for a "purpose item in respect of which the Parliament has power to make laws". This item means that every law supported by s 51(xxxi) must not be supported item by any other additional legislative power. Property The High Court of Australia item has taken a wide view of the concept of "property". Several members item of the court took the opportunity to consider the meaning of the item term property in Minister of State for the Army v Dalziel (1944). item Justice Starke said the term includes: "every species of valuable right and item interest including real and personal property, incorporeal hereditaments such as rents and item services, rights-of-way, rights of profit or use in land of another, and item choses in action. Justice McTiernan confirmed the term property extends to tangible item and intangible property. An example of the breadth of the concept of item property in section 51(xxxi) is provided by Bank of New South Wales item v Commonwealth (the Bank Nationalisation Case). In that case, Federal legislation contemplated item the acquisition of private banks through vesting of shares in private banks item in the Commonwealth, and later the appointment of directors by the Governor item of the Commonwealth Bank. Justice Dixon characterised the provisions as removing effective item control over the property of the private banks. He concluded that this item was, in the essential sense, an acquisition of a proprietary right. While item statutory licences have sometimes been equated with proprietary interests, the removal of item rights enjoyed under a statutory licence does not typically constitute an acquisition item of property within section 51(xxxi), as licence conditions are inherently susceptible to item change. Acquisition For the purposes of section 51(xxxi), property must have been item acquired by somebody, and the acquisition must be for a Commonwealth purpose. item This is in contrast to the Fifth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, item where the destination does not matter – it is enough that the item holder of property has been deprived of it. Thus in JT International item SA v Commonwealth the High Court held that the Commonwealth's plain tobacco item packaging laws, which restricted the plaintiff's use of its trademark, did not item involve the Commonwealth acquiring any property. Similarly in Cunningham v Commonwealth the item High Court held that changes to the retiring allowances and life Gold item Pass for retired members of Parliament were not an acquisition of property. item In P J Magennis Pty Ltd v Commonwealth the High Court held item that a grant to NSW which was tied to NSW compulsorily acquiring item property was invalid as an acquisition of property upon terms which were item not just. The validity of a grant in the absence of a item requirement to acquire property was upheld in the later case of Pye item v Renshaw. Just terms Typically, a determination of just terms based on item the market value of the property at the time of acquisition will item be sufficient to satisfy the requirement of just terms. Unlike the "just item compensation" requirement in the American Fifth Amendment, however, "just terms" imports no item equivalence of market value. The arrangements offered must be "fair", or such item that a legislature could reasonably regard them as "fair". However, this judgment item of "fairness" must take account of all the interests affected, not just item those of the dispossessed owner. The requirement of "just terms" does not item necessarily require that a compensation package be presented as part of the item acquisition scheme. It is sufficient that the scheme provides adequate procedures for item determining fair compensation. However, the Court may scrutinise such procedures closely to item ensure their adequacy. There may be some acquisitions of property to which item section 51(xxxi) does not apply, such as those made under laws supported item exclusively by section 122 of the Constitution. Section 51(xxxi) is an exception item to the norm for interpretation of the subsections of section 51, that item one grant of power cannot be used to "read down" another. In item this case, however, the Court will not allow another grant of power item to be read so broadly as to circumvent the specific limitation to item the power granted by section 51(xxxi).
